sections.b:
The word go'el and its verb appear more than 20 times in Ruth's 85 verses, more often for its length than in any other book. Naomi first realizes that Boaz is "one of our family redeemers" (2:20). Ruth asks him to act as one by marrying her (3:9). Boaz admits a closer redeemer has the first right (3:12) and settles the matter at the town gate (4:1–10).

In the Law, the redeemer bought back land (Leviticus 25:25) and relatives sold as slaves (Leviticus 25:47–49), and avenged murder (Numbers 35:19). No law says he must marry a widow; that was the brother-in-law's duty (Deuteronomy 25:5–10). Ruth joins the two, and the nearer redeemer accepts that the land comes with the marriage. In the end the women call the newborn Obed Naomi's go'el (4:14).
sections.refs: Ruth 2:20; Ruth 3:9; Ruth 3:12–13; Ruth 4:1–10; Ruth 4:14; Leviticus 25:25; Leviticus 25:47–49; Deuteronomy 25:5–10

sections.b: Isaiah 40–55 calls God Israel's Go'el about ten times: "Your Redeemer is the Holy One of Israel" (Isaiah 41:14). Job's "I know that my redeemer lives" (Job 19:25) uses the same word. Christian readers have long seen Boaz as a picture of Christ, the near relative who pays the price for those who cannot redeem themselves (Galatians 4:4–5; Hebrews 2:11–17). Jewish readers see in the story the human side of God's own redeeming love.
sections.refs: Isaiah 41:14; Isaiah 43:1; Isaiah 54:5; Job 19:25; Galatians 4:4–5; Hebrews 2:11–17; Ruth 4:14

common: A redeemer had to marry his relative's widow.
uncommon: The last redeemer in the book is not Boaz but the baby, Obed (4:14).
The nearer redeemer did nothing wrong; he simply would not pay the cost.

claude.title: The redeemer who loses his name
claude.body: My own observation, building on common ones: the book measures redemption by names. The nearer redeemer refuses to "raise up the dead man's name" (4:5, 10) and is left as "So-and-so" (4:1). Boaz, who raises up Mahlon's name, is remembered by name in the line of David and of Jesus. Redemption in Ruth is the work of keeping another person's name alive at your own cost.

sections.b:
Ruth uses hesed only three times, but it is the theme of the book. Naomi prays that the LORD will show her daughters-in-law hesed as they have shown it to the dead and to her (1:8). She blesses the one "who has not abandoned his faithful love for the living and the dead" (2:20), a phrase that can mean God or Boaz. Boaz praises Ruth's last hesed as greater than her first (3:10).

Each act goes beyond duty: Ruth stays with Naomi, Boaz gives far more than the gleaning law asks, and Ruth seeks a husband who can carry on her dead husband's family. The rabbis said the whole book was written to teach the reward of hesed (Ruth Rabbah 2:14).
sections.refs: Ruth 1:8; Ruth 2:20; Ruth 3:10; Exodus 34:6–7; Micah 6:8

uncommon: In Ruth the person most praised for hesed is a Moabite.
The ambiguity of 2:20 may be deliberate: God's hesed and Boaz's hesed are the same act.

sections.b:
Naomi has the custom in mind when she says she has no more sons for her daughters-in-law to marry (1:11–13). Ruth's case is not a strict levirate marriage, since Boaz is not Mahlon's brother, but the language of Deuteronomy 25 runs through chapter 4: "to raise up the dead man's name on his inheritance" (4:5, 10; compare Deuteronomy 25:6–7), a sandal (4:7–8; compare Deuteronomy 25:9) and the elders at the gate (4:1–2; Deuteronomy 25:7). The sandal here confirms a transfer rather than shaming the man who refuses.

Scholars disagree whether Ruth shows an older, wider family custom, a local practice or a creative use of the law. The town's blessing compares the marriage with Tamar's (4:12), the other levirate story in Judah's family.
sections.refs: Ruth 1:11–13; Ruth 4:5–10; Ruth 4:12; Deuteronomy 25:5–10; Genesis 38:8–26

sections.h: Moab in the book of Ruth
sections.b:
Ruth calls its heroine "the Moabite" again and again (1:22; 2:2, 21; 4:5, 10). Elimelech's family goes to "the fields of Moab" in a famine (1:1), his sons marry Moabite women (1:4), and Orpah goes back "to her people and to her gods" (1:15), probably the god Chemosh (Numbers 21:29). Against that background, Ruth's "your God is my God" (1:16) is a real change of loyalty.

The story has to be read beside Moab's harsh place in the rest of the Bible: its origin in Lot's daughters (Genesis 19:30–38), Balaam and Baal-peor (Numbers 22–25) and the ban of Deuteronomy 23:3–6. The rabbis said the ban applied to Moabite men, not women (Mishnah, Yevamot 8:3). David later sent his parents to the king of Moab for safety (1 Samuel 22:3–4).
sections.refs: Ruth 1:1–4; Ruth 1:15–16; Ruth 1:22; Ruth 2:2; Ruth 4:5; Ruth 4:10; Genesis 19:30–38; Deuteronomy 23:3–6; 1 Samuel 22:3–4

uncommon: The book never criticizes Moab or Moabites; the only judgment on Moab's religion is Ruth's own choice to leave it.

sections.b:
Ruth begins with no bread in the "house of bread" (1:1) and the LORD giving bread again (1:6). The whole town is stirred when Naomi returns (1:19), the harvest takes place in its fields, and its gate is where Boaz settles the case (4:1–11). The townspeople bless Boaz to "make a name in Bethlehem" and "do worthy things in Ephrathah" (4:11), the old clan name that Micah later uses for the birthplace of a ruler (Micah 5:2).

By ending with David, Ruth makes Bethlehem David's town (1 Samuel 16:1–13; 17:12). The Gospels place Jesus' birth there (Matthew 2:1–6; Luke 2:4–11).
sections.refs: Ruth 1:1–2; Ruth 1:6; Ruth 1:19; Ruth 4:11; Micah 5:2; 1 Samuel 17:12; Matthew 2:1–6; Luke 2:4–11

uncommon: In Judges, Bethlehem is linked to two of Israel's ugliest stories (Judges 17–19); Ruth gives the town a new reputation.

sections.b: Ruth 2 is the Bible's fullest picture of the gleaning laws at work. Ruth fits every category the law protects: poor, foreign and widowed (Leviticus 19:9–10; Deuteronomy 24:19–22). She still needs a landowner's goodwill (2:2), and she may have asked for more than the usual right by gleaning "among the sheaves" (2:7). Boaz grants that, protects her from harassment, gives her water and lunch, and tells his men to pull stalks out of the bundles for her (2:8–16). By evening she has about an ephah of barley (2:17).
sections.refs: Ruth 2:2–3; Ruth 2:7–17; Ruth 2:23; Leviticus 19:9–10; Leviticus 23:22; Deuteronomy 24:19–22

uncommon: Gleaning was a legal right of the poor, not a favor; what Boaz added was the favor.

sections.b: Ruth ends with David's name, twice (4:17, 22). Through Ruth and Boaz's son Obed, David has a Moabite great-grandmother. Many scholars think the book was written to show that David's family, foreign blood and all, was honorable and guided by God. It may also explain why David sent his parents to the king of Moab when Saul hunted him (1 Samuel 22:3–4). The genealogy in 4:18–22 is repeated in 1 Chronicles 2:5–15 and in Jesus' family lines (Matthew 1:3–6; Luke 3:31–33).
sections.refs: Ruth 4:17–22; 1 Samuel 16:1–13; 1 Samuel 22:3–4; 1 Chronicles 2:5–15; Matthew 1:5–6

common: Ruth was David's grandmother (she was his great-grandmother).

sections.b:
Ruth is a Moabite widow who refuses to leave her mother-in-law (1:14–17), works all day to feed her (2:2–18), follows and then improves on Naomi's bold plan (3:1–9), and becomes Boaz's wife and Obed's mother (4:13). Boaz calls her "a woman of worth" (3:11), the phrase of Proverbs 31:10, and the women say she is "worth more to you than seven sons" (4:15).

Jewish tradition honors her as the model convert and as "the mother of royalty"; the Talmud says she lived to see Solomon (Bava Batra 91b). Christians remember her in Matthew's genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:5), one of four women named there.
sections.refs: Ruth 1:14–17; Ruth 2:2–18; Ruth 3:1–11; Ruth 4:13–15; Proverbs 31:10; Matthew 1:5

common: Ruth seduced Boaz on the threshing floor.
uncommon: Ruth uses the name of Israel's God in an oath (1:17) before she has ever seen Israel.

sections.b:
Naomi loses her husband and sons (1:3–5), comes home and asks to be called Mara, "Bitter" (1:20), and says the LORD has brought her back "empty" (1:21). Her mood turns when she hears Boaz's name (2:20). She makes the plan for the threshing floor (3:1–4) and waits with confidence for the result (3:18). At the end she holds Ruth's son in her lap, and the women say, "A son is born to Naomi" (4:16–17).

Readers differ over Naomi. Some see a model of honest lament like Job; some see a grieving woman who overlooks Ruth at first (1:21); most see a character who changes, and the book lets her change.

Boaz is introduced as "a man of great worth" from Elimelech's clan (2:1). He greets his workers with a blessing (2:4), protects and feeds Ruth (2:8–16), blesses her in the LORD's name (2:12; 3:10), keeps his word without taking advantage of her at night (3:10–14), and settles the case lawfully at the gate (4:1–10). He is listed among Jesus' ancestors (Matthew 1:5; Luke 3:32). Some rabbis identified him with the judge Ibzan of Bethlehem (Judges 12:8–10; Talmud, Bava Batra 91a), but the Bible does not say this.
sections.refs: Ruth 2:1–16; Ruth 3:10–14; Ruth 4:1–13; Judges 12:8–10; 1 Kings 7:21; Matthew 1:5

common: Boaz was a young man in love.
uncommon: Boaz calls Ruth "my daughter" and praises her for not seeking younger men (3:10), suggesting a sizable age gap.

sections.h: God behind the scenes in Ruth
sections.b: God never speaks or appears in Ruth. The narrator credits him directly only twice: he gives bread (1:6) and conception (4:13). Yet the characters bless and pray in his name constantly (1:8–9; 2:4, 12, 19–20; 3:10, 13; 4:11–12, 14), and Ruth's "chance" arrival in Boaz's field (2:3) is told with a wink. Naomi blames God for her losses (1:13, 20–21); by 2:20 she praises his faithful love. Many readers see Ruth as the Bible's clearest picture of providence through ordinary people, alongside Joseph (Genesis 50:20) and Esther.
sections.refs: Ruth 1:6; Ruth 1:13; Ruth 1:20–21; Ruth 2:3; Ruth 2:20; Ruth 4:13; Genesis 50:20; Proverbs 16:9; Esther 4:14

uncommon: Naomi's complaint against God is never corrected in the book; it is answered by events.

sections.b: Boaz blesses Ruth by the LORD, "under whose wings you have come for refuge" (2:12). At midnight Ruth asks Boaz, "Spread the wing of your cloak over your servant" (3:9), using the same word, kanaf. To spread one's garment over a woman meant marriage (Ezekiel 16:8; compare Deuteronomy 22:30). The two verses together suggest that God's protection reaches Ruth through Boaz's commitment.
sections.refs: Ruth 2:12; Ruth 3:9; Ezekiel 16:8; Deuteronomy 22:30; Psalm 17:8; Psalm 36:7; Psalm 91:4; Matthew 23:37

sections.b:
Ruth calls herself a nokhriyyah, "foreigner" (2:10), and the narrator keeps calling her "the Moabite." Her vow, "Your people are my people, and your God is my God" (1:16), joins people and faith together. Boaz praises her for leaving her land like Abraham (2:11–12), the town blesses her to be like Rachel and Leah (4:11), and she becomes David's great-grandmother (4:17).

The book sits in tension with laws and reforms that kept Moabites out (Deuteronomy 23:3–6; Ezra 9–10; Nehemiah 13:1–3, 23–27). The rabbis resolved it by limiting the ban to Moabite men (Mishnah, Yevamot 8:3). Many critical scholars read the book as a deliberate answer to Ezra and Nehemiah; others see it simply as a story of how a faithful outsider was welcomed. Christians often connect it with the prophets' welcome of foreigners (Isaiah 56:3–7) and the Gentiles' inclusion in the church (Ephesians 2:11–19).
sections.refs: Ruth 1:16; Ruth 2:10–12; Ruth 4:11; Ruth 4:17; Deuteronomy 23:3–6; Ezra 9:1–2; Nehemiah 13:23–27; Isaiah 56:3–7; Ephesians 2:11–19

common: Ruth was the first convert to Judaism.
uncommon: The book never resolves the tension with Deuteronomy 23:3; it simply tells the story and lets the reader weigh it.

sections.h: Why Ruth is read at Shavuot
sections.b: Ruth is the scroll read in synagogues at Shavuot. The story runs from the start of barley harvest (1:22) to the end of wheat harvest (2:23), roughly the seven weeks the festival marks (Leviticus 23:15–16; Deuteronomy 16:9). Later Jewish tradition gave further reasons: Shavuot remembers the giving of the Torah at Sinai, and Ruth's acceptance of Israel's God matches Israel's acceptance of the covenant; and David, Ruth's great-grandson, was said to have been born and to have died on Shavuot.
sections.refs: Ruth 1:22; Ruth 2:23; Leviticus 23:15–21; Deuteronomy 16:9–12; Exodus 19:1; Acts 2:1

sections.b: The elders bless Boaz: "May your house be like the house of Perez, whom Tamar bore to Judah" (4:12). The two stories mirror each other. Both women are widows with no child; both are outsiders (Tamar is probably Canaanite, Ruth a Moabite); both take a bold, risky step toward an older man of Judah's family; both are declared righteous or worthy by that man (Genesis 38:26; Ruth 3:10–11); and both bear a son who continues the line. The genealogy then begins with Perez (4:18). Harold Fisch and others have traced this pattern back to Lot's daughters, the mothers of Moab (Genesis 19:30–38).
sections.refs: Ruth 4:12; Ruth 4:18; Genesis 38:6–30; Genesis 19:30–38; Matthew 1:3

sections.h: Ruth in the days of the judges
sections.b: Ruth opens "in the days when the judges ruled" (1:1), but it shows a very different side of that age from the book of Judges: ordinary people who keep the law, bless one another in the LORD's name and act with hesed. Both books feature Bethlehem (Judges 17:7; 19:1), and both end by pointing toward a king (Judges 21:25; Ruth 4:17). The aside "this was the custom in Israel in earlier times" (4:7) shows the book was written later, looking back on the period.
sections.refs: Ruth 1:1; Ruth 4:7; Ruth 4:17; Judges 17:6–7; Judges 19:1; Judges 21:25

sections.h: The LORD and the Almighty in Ruth
sections.b: The divine name YHWH appears 18 times in Ruth, nearly always in blessings, prayers and oaths: "The LORD be with you" (2:4), "May the LORD pay you back" (2:12), "as the LORD lives" (3:13). Ruth the Moabite swears by it (1:17). Naomi pairs it with Shaddai, "the Almighty," in her complaint (1:20–21), the name often used in Job for God in suffering. Elohim, "God," appears in Ruth's vow (1:16) and in "the LORD, the God of Israel" (2:12).
sections.refs: Ruth 1:16–17; Ruth 1:20–21; Ruth 2:4; Ruth 2:12; Ruth 3:13; Exodus 3:14–15; Exodus 6:3; Job 27:2

sections.b: Ruth has about a dozen Ketiv/Qere notes. Several are old spellings of "you" for a woman that look like "I" (3:3, 4). Two are words read aloud though not written ("to me" in 3:5 and 3:17), and one is a word written but not read (3:12). Two change the meaning: 2:1, "relative" or "acquaintance," and 4:5, where the written text says "I acquire" and the reading tradition "you acquire" Ruth. The second, with another small problem in the same verse, makes 4:5 the hardest verse in the book.
sections.refs: Ruth 2:1; Ruth 3:3–5; Ruth 3:12; Ruth 3:17; Ruth 4:5

sections.b: Ruth begins with three widows: Naomi, Orpah and Ruth (1:3–5). Naomi assumes the young women's only hope is remarriage in their mothers' houses (1:8–9) and that she herself has no future (1:11–13, 20–21). The book then shows the protections the law gave widows working in practice: gleaning (2:2; Deuteronomy 24:19–21), the redeemer (2:20; Leviticus 25:25) and the family duty to raise up a dead man's name (4:5, 10; Deuteronomy 25:5–6). It also shows their limits: without Boaz's goodwill, all of these could fail.
sections.refs: Ruth 1:3–13; Ruth 1:20–21; Ruth 2:2; Ruth 2:20; Ruth 4:5; Ruth 4:10; Deuteronomy 24:19–21; Deuteronomy 25:5–6; Exodus 22:22–24

sections.h: The night on Boaz's threshing floor
sections.b: Naomi sends Ruth to the threshing floor at night, where Boaz is winnowing barley and will sleep by his grain (3:2–7). The setting was risky: Hosea links threshing floors with prostitution (Hosea 9:1), and the scene's words ("uncover," "feet," "lie down") can carry sexual meaning. Most interpreters, Jewish and Christian, conclude that the narrator uses that tension to show Boaz's and Ruth's integrity: he protects her and sends her home before dawn with grain (3:13–15).
sections.refs: Ruth 3:2–15; Hosea 9:1; 2 Samuel 24:18–25; 2 Chronicles 3:1

sections.b: Naomi prays that the LORD will give her daughters-in-law "rest in the house of a husband" (1:9), using menuchah, the word for Israel's rest in the land (Deuteronomy 12:9). In 3:1 she sets out to find "a place of rest" for Ruth herself. The chapter ends with Boaz unable to "rest" until he has settled the matter (3:18). In Ruth, rest means a secure home, food and a future, received through faithful people.
sections.refs: Ruth 1:9; Ruth 3:1; Ruth 3:18; Deuteronomy 12:9; Psalm 95:11; Hebrews 4:9

sections.b:
Ruth ends with ten generations from Perez to David (4:18–22), using the "these are the generations" formula of Genesis. The list reappears in 1 Chronicles 2:5–15, Matthew 1:3–6 and Luke 3:31–33. Boaz stands seventh and David tenth. Because Nahshon lived in Moses' day, most scholars think the list skips some names, as ancient genealogies often did.

Matthew names Ruth as one of four mothers in Jesus' line, with Tamar, Rahab and Bathsheba, and adds that Rahab was Boaz's mother (Matthew 1:5). Many readers think he lists these women to show that God's plan always included outsiders.
sections.refs: Ruth 4:18–22; 1 Chronicles 2:5–15; Matthew 1:3–6; Luke 3:31–33; Genesis 5:1

sections.b: In the King James Version, "mercy" often stands for the Hebrew hesed, faithful love, which the KJV renders "mercy" about 150 times, as in Psalm 136's refrain "for his mercy endureth for ever." The Septuagint usually translates hesed with eleos, "mercy," the word the New Testament uses. So when an Old Testament verse speaks of God's "mercy" in the KJV, it is often hesed. Ruth shows hesed at work among people: Naomi prays for it (Ruth 1:8), Boaz shows it (Ruth 2:20) and Ruth is praised for it (Ruth 3:10). See the separate page on hesed.
sections.refs: Psalm 136:1; Ruth 1:8; Ruth 2:20; Ruth 3:10; Micah 6:8

sections.b: Ruth is the Bible's great harvest story. Naomi comes home "at the beginning of the barley harvest" (Ruth 1:22), after a famine. Ruth gleans behind the reapers as the law allowed (Ruth 2:2–3; Leviticus 19:9–10), eats roasted grain with the workers (Ruth 2:14), beats out an ephah of barley (Ruth 2:17), and gleans until the end of the barley and wheat harvests (Ruth 2:23). Boaz winnows his barley at the threshing floor (Ruth 3:2) and sends Ruth home with six measures of it (Ruth 3:15). The movement of the book from empty to full follows the movement of the farm year from famine to harvest.
sections.refs: Ruth 1:1; Ruth 1:22; Ruth 2:2–23; Ruth 3:2; Ruth 3:15; Leviticus 19:9–10; Leviticus 23:10–22

sections.b: Ruth's Hebrew text is well preserved. Four small Dead Sea Scroll copies survive (2QRuth-a, 2QRuth-b, 4QRuth-a, 4QRuth-b), from roughly the first century BC to the first century AD, and they agree closely with the Masoretic Text. The Septuagint is close to the Hebrew, with a few explanatory additions (Ruth 1:14; 4:8) and a different form of the blessing in Ruth 4:11. The Masoretic Text has about a dozen Ketiv/Qere notes, two of which change the meaning (Ruth 2:1; 4:5); Ruth 4:5 is the hardest textual problem in the book.
sections.refs: Ruth 1:14; Ruth 2:1; Ruth 4:5; Ruth 4:8; Ruth 4:11
